raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 2-year-old girl presented with 1 week of progressive weakness and limping. Physical examination revealed lethargy, pallor, and widespread petechiae. Laboratory evaluation demonstrated anemia (hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (39,000 /mm3), and leukocytosis (20,000 /mm3) with 95% circulating lymphoblasts. Peripheral smear confirmed blasts, and bone marrow aspiration with flow cytometric analysis established the diagnosis of B-cell ALL. A port catheter was placed, and induction chemotherapy per the COG AALL-1731 protocol was initiated, with remission achieved at the end of induction.
On day 10 of intensive consolidation therapy, the patient developed febrile neutropenia. Despite sequential broad-spectrum antimicrobials (piperacillin-tazobactam, followed by teicoplanin and levofloxacin), fever persisted. Blood, urine, stool, and throat cultures remained negative, and serum galactomannan assays were also negative. Because fever continued beyond 96 h, thoracic CT imaging was obtained, revealing a 15 x 10-mm pleura-adjacent consolidation in the left upper lobe and a 3.5-mm right lower lobe nodule with a surrounding ground-glass halo (Figure 1). These findings raised suspicion for early angioinvasive fungal infection, prompting initiation of liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB, 3 mg/kg/day), after which the fever resolved.
On day 40 of consolidation therapy, while still receiving L-AmB, the patient developed sudden massive hemoptysis, necessitating transfer to the pediatric intensive care unit. Neutrophil and platelet counts and coagulation parameters were within normal limits, reducing suspicion of hematologic causes of bleeding. Empirical voriconazole was added, and ENT examination did not reveal an upper airway source. Contrast-enhanced thoracic CT demonstrated a saccular pseudoaneurysm arising from the proximal left subclavian artery, surrounded by thrombus, extending into the adjacent lung parenchyma, and causing compressive atelectasis. These findings were highly consistent with a mycotic pseudoaneurysm secondary to angioinvasive aspergillosis.
A multidisciplinary meeting involving pediatric hematology, infectious diseases, pediatric ICU, pediatric surgery, and cardiovascular surgery teams concluded that urgent surgical intervention was required due to the high risk of aneurysmal rupture. The patient underwent left upper lobe segmentectomy with complete excision of the pseudoaneurysm, and the left subclavian artery was reconstructed using an autologous vein graft (Figure 2). Gross pathology revealed consolidated lung parenchyma with an 18-mm cavitary lesion.
Microbiologic evaluation showed no growth in tissue cultures, and serum galactomannan remained negative. Histopathologic examination demonstrated hemorrhage, necrosis, and suppurative inflammation, but no fungal elements were visible on periodic acid-schiff (PAS) or Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) staining:a well-recognized limitation in cases of angioinvasive aspergillosis following antifungal exposure or significant tissue necrosis (Figure 3). However, Aspergillus-specific PCR performed on excised tissue was positive for A. flavus, confirming the etiologic organism. Based on host factors (ALL with neutropenia), radiologic evidence of vascular invasion, and positive fungal PCR, the case fulfilled European organization for research and treatment of cancer (EORTC)/mycoses study group (MSG) criteria for probable invasive aspergillosis (IA) with vascular involvement.
Postoperative CT angiography showed complete resolution of the pseudoaneurysm. Low-dose aspirin (5 mg/kg/day) was initiated to prevent graft thrombosis and was recommended as lifelong therapy by the cardiology and cardiovascular surgery teams. Dual antifungal therapy with L-AmB and voriconazole was continued for 60 days, and long-term voriconazole prophylaxis was maintained for 17 months throughout consolidation and maintenance therapy. Discontinuation was considered once imaging remained stable and the patient reached day 71 of the third maintenance cycle.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-year-old girl with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia developed persistent febrile neutropenia on day 10 of consolidation chemotherapy followed on day 40 by sudden massive hemoptysis.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with 1 week of progressive weakness, limping, lethargy, pallor, and petechiae, and was diagnosed with B-cell ALL, achieving remission after COG AALL-1731 induction chemotherapy. On day 10 of intensive consolidation therapy, she developed febrile neutropenia refractory to >96 hours of broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam, teicoplanin, levofloxacin); thoracic CT showed a left upper lobe consolidation and right lower lobe halo-sign nodule, and fever resolved after starting liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day). However, on day 40 of consolidation therapy while still on liposomal amphotericin B, she experienced sudden massive hemoptysis requiring pediatric ICU admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy prior to diagnosis of B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) treated per COG AALL-1731 protocol.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive initially for weakness, limping, lethargy, and petechiae, then persistent neutropenic fever (day 10 of consolidation) and sudden massive hemoptysis (day 40 of consolidation).

objective.physical_examination: At initial ALL diagnosis: lethargy, pallor, and widespread petechiae. At day 40 massive hemoptysis: ENT examination showed no upper airway bleeding source.
objective.routine_investigations: At initial ALL diagnosis: hemoglobin 9.3 g/dL, platelets 39,000/mm3, WBC 20,000/mm3 with 95% circulating lymphoblasts, and bone marrow flow cytometry confirming B-cell ALL. During day 10 febrile neutropenia: blood, urine, stool, and throat cultures were negative. At day 40 hemoptysis: neutrophil count, platelet count, and coagulation parameters were within normal limits.
objective.advanced_workup: Serial serum galactomannan assays were negative. Day 10 consolidation thoracic CT showed a 15 x 10 mm pleura-adjacent consolidation in the left upper lobe and a 3.5 mm right lower lobe nodule with a surrounding ground-glass halo sign. Day 40 contrast-enhanced thoracic CT demonstrated a saccular mycotic pseudoaneurysm arising from the proximal left subclavian artery surrounded by thrombus, extending into the adjacent left upper lobe parenchyma and causing compressive atelectasis. Following urgent left upper lobe segmentectomy (resecting an 18-mm cavitary lesion) and left subclavian artery reconstruction with an autologous vein graft, tissue fungal cultures and PAS/GMS stains were negative (attributed to prior L-AmB therapy and extensive necrosis), but Aspergillus-specific PCR on the excised tissue was positive for Aspergillus flavus.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Probable/tissue-PCR-confirmed angioinvasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus flavus) complicated by a life-threatening left subclavian artery mycotic pseudoaneurysm and massive hemoptysis during consolidation chemotherapy for pediatric B-cell ALL, confirmed by early CT halo sign, CT angiography showing subclavian pseudoaneurysm invading the left upper lobe, and positive Aspergillus flavus PCR on resected tissue. Treated with urgent surgical pseudoaneurysm excision, autologous vein graft reconstruction of the left subclavian artery, and left upper lobe segmentectomy, combined with 60 days of dual antifungal therapy (liposomal amphotericin B plus voriconazole), 17 months of maintenance voriconazole prophylaxis throughout chemotherapy, and lifelong low-dose aspirin (5 mg/kg/day), with complete resolution of the pseudoaneurysm on follow-up CT angiography.
